speaker: Narrator
text: Rain on old glass. A castle of a thousand windows, and only a few of them lit.

speaker: Narrator
text: Every old school keeps a secret. This one keeps it under a tower, and the secret has begun to ring.

speaker: Narrator
text: You, Kringer, of Gryffindor, have been at the castle long enough to stop getting lost on the way to breakfast, and not nearly long enough to know where it keeps its shadows.

speaker: Narrator
text: You, Kringer, of Slytherin, have been at the castle long enough to stop getting lost on the way to breakfast, and not nearly long enough to know where it keeps its shadows.

speaker: Narrator
text: You, Kringer, of Ravenclaw, have been at the castle long enough to stop getting lost on the way to breakfast, and not nearly long enough to know where it keeps its shadows.

speaker: Narrator
text: You, Kringer, of Hufflepuff, have been at the castle long enough to stop getting lost on the way to breakfast, and not nearly long enough to know where it keeps its shadows.

speaker: Narrator
text: Dinner tonight was loud and warm, the way it always is. You laughed at something. You fell asleep to the sound of rain.

speaker: Narrator
text: Whatever happens next, you will remember this as the last ordinary evening.

speaker: Narrator
text: The clock above the Gryffindor dormitory fireplace shows a few minutes past midnight when you wake. Something has pulled you out of sleep, and it takes a moment to understand that it is a sound: a deep, hollow note, like a bell rung at the bottom of a lake.

speaker: Narrator
text: The clock above the Slytherin dormitory fireplace shows a few minutes past midnight when you wake. Something has pulled you out of sleep, and it takes a moment to understand that it is a sound: a deep, hollow note, like a bell rung at the bottom of a lake.

speaker: Narrator
text: The clock above the Ravenclaw dormitory fireplace shows a few minutes past midnight when you wake. Something has pulled you out of sleep, and it takes a moment to understand that it is a sound: a deep, hollow note, like a bell rung at the bottom of a lake.

speaker: Narrator
text: The clock above the Hufflepuff dormitory fireplace shows a few minutes past midnight when you wake. Something has pulled you out of sleep, and it takes a moment to understand that it is a sound: a deep, hollow note, like a bell rung at the bottom of a lake.

speaker: Narrator
text: Nobody else stirs. In the next bed Pip Marlowe lies with his mouth slightly open, breathing slow and even, one hand curled around the wrapper of a chocolate frog he must have fallen asleep eating.

speaker: Narrator
text: You have stood in this room before. You remember how this night ends, and you remember what it cost.

speaker: Narrator
text: The note comes again. This time you feel it in your breastbone, as if the castle has a pulse and has just skipped a beat.

speaker: Narrator
text: You shake Pip by the shoulder. His skin is cold as a stone in a stream, and he does not respond. His eyes move fast beneath the lids, the way eyes do when someone is dreaming something they cannot climb out of.

speaker: Narrator
text: You whisper his name three times. Nothing. But when the bell tolls again, his fingers tighten on the chocolate frog wrapper, as if something has taken hold of him and he is holding on.

speaker: Narrator
text: Beyond the window the grounds lie silver under the moon. High above the rooftops, at the top of Hollow Tower, the old clock tower that has been sealed for fifty years, a pale light flickers.

speaker: Narrator
text: Each time the bell tolls the light pulses, and a thin mist seeps out of the tower windows and drifts down toward the dormitories like breath on cold glass.

speaker: Narrator
text: You count the tolls. Seven. Then silence. Then it begins again, and you notice that the gaps are getting shorter.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pip does not wake. The whole castle sleeps too deeply, too evenly, and somewhere above it the bell keeps its patient time. You have three options, and none of them is safe.

speaker: Narrator
text: You slip into the corridors with your wand in your fist and no light. The castle is another place at night. Portraits breathe in their frames, suits of armour seem to be listening, and the air tastes of cold iron.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the foot of the tower stairs the silence thickens. The sound of your footsteps leaves your feet and does not arrive at your ears, as if something is eating it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ahead, around the corner, a light swings. Someone is coming.

speaker: Narrator
text: From the shadow of an alcove you watch two lights part ways. One is a warm, swinging lantern heading down toward the kitchen stairs. The other is no light at all: a hooded figure with a ring of keys that chimes faintly, crossing the courtyard arch toward the tower.

speaker: Narrator
text: You have time to follow only one. Or to go straight to the door they’re both avoiding.

speaker: Narrator
text: The lantern belongs to an old man in a patched coat, a brass spyglass hanging on a cord around his neck. He stops as though he had been expecting you, then seems embarrassed to be caught expecting.

speaker: Quill
text: Oh. Oh, you hear it too. Forgive me, I’m, Quill. Night archivist. Nobody asks what an archivist does at night, which is lucky, because mostly it’s listening.

speaker: Narrator
text: He lowers his voice.

speaker: Quill
text: I have waited fifty years for someone else to hear it.

speaker: Narrator
text: He takes your elbow with surprising firmness and steers you away from the tower.

speaker: Quill
text: Not tonight. The bell is hungry, and you are rather small to feed it. Come to the archive tomorrow. Bring questions. Bring tea, if you can steal any.

speaker: Narrator
text: You keep to the shadows and follow the chiming keys. The figure unlocks the tower door without hesitation, slips inside, and pulls it shut behind them. You wait. The bell tolls above you, twice, and the door opens again.

speaker: Narrator
text: The figure comes out coughing into a sleeve, a hard dry cough you almost recognise, and locks up. They pass your hiding place close enough that you smell pipe smoke and lamp oil. You never see a face.

speaker: Narrator
text: The tower door is black oak banded with iron, and cold radiates from it like winter from a cellar. Your hand is on the handle before you decide to move it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Beneath your palm the wood hums, low and patient, and the hum finds the bones of your wrist. For a moment you hear something that is not the bell. A voice, almost: a lullaby with its words worn smooth. Then you snatch your hand away and the silence rushes back in.

speaker: Narrator
text: A lantern beam catches you square in the chest.

speaker: Harrow
text: Well, well.

speaker: Narrator
text: It’s Harrow, the caretaker, lamp in one hand and a face that hasn’t smiled since before you were born. His coat smells of pipe smoke.

speaker: Harrow
text: Out of bed past midnight, Kringer. Explain yourself.

speaker: Narrator
text: You tell him everything: Pip, the bell, the light on the tower. Harrow listens without a word, his jaw working. When you finish he lets out a long breath through his nose.

speaker: Harrow
text: The bell has rung before,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Harrow
text: I was young. I told myself I dreamed it.

speaker: Narrator
text: He jerks his head toward the stairs.

speaker: Harrow
text: Get to bed, Kringer. And when you can, talk to Quill in the archive before you talk to anyone else with a title.

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow looks straight through you.

speaker: Harrow
text: Sleepwalkers don’t carry wands.

speaker: Narrator
text: You spend the rest of the night polishing brass plaques in the trophy room while the bell tolls faintly through the walls.

speaker: Narrator
text: By dawn your name is in his book: first warning. One more, and a letter goes home.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela Voss, sixth-year prefect, opens her door in a dressing gown, hair wild, a book already open in one hand. She does not tell you to go back to bed. She listens to every word with her eyebrows slowly rising.

speaker: Mirela
text: Four last night. Six tonight,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says.

speaker: Mirela
text: Asleep, all of them. Calm as lambs, cold as slate. The staff are calling it a stomach bug.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her mouth thins.

speaker: Mirela
text: I call it something else.

speaker: Narrator
text: She looks at you properly for the first time.

speaker: Mirela
text: You heard the bell. Most people don’t. That makes you either very useful or very unlucky. Possibly both.

speaker: Narrator
text: She takes you the long way, through the library gallery and down the servants’ stair, because she has already mapped which corridors the portraits gossip in. At the foot of Hollow Tower a door of black oak waits, banded with iron.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela opens her notebook and reads off times in a flat voice.

speaker: Mirela
text: Tolls every eleven minutes, sometimes ten. It’s speeding up.

speaker: Narrator
text: She studies the door.

speaker: Mirela
text: I’d like to know if it’s locked or just unwelcoming.

speaker: Narrator
text: Your fingers close on the iron ring and the door hums through your arm. Something pulls, gently, like a current under smooth water. You stand there and do not let go for far too long, and then you do.

speaker: Mirela
text: Interesting,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Mirela quietly, though her face has lost its colour.

speaker: Mirela
text: You held on longer than I would have.

speaker: Narrator
text: The hum finds you before you have finished reaching for the handle. The edges of the corridor blur and your knees go soft. Mirela catches you by the collar and hauls you from the door like a kitten from a pond.

speaker: Mirela
text: That,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says through her teeth,

speaker: Mirela
text: is not a lock.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela whispers a lock-breaker and the air before the door sours. The spell comes back on itself as a puff of cold dust, and her wand hand goes numb. She flexes her fingers, quiet and calculating.

speaker: Mirela
text: Well,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says.

speaker: Mirela
text: It listens, at least.

speaker: Narrator
text: At dawn you stand in the doorway of the hospital wing and stop. Every bed is full, and every sleeper is peaceful. Matron Hale moves between them with a clipboard and an expression like a closed door.

speaker: Matron Hale
text: Sleeping sickness,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says before you can ask.

speaker: Matron Hale
text: Nothing to be done but rest and fluids. Professor Ashgrove has been very kind about it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her eyes flick away on the last word.

speaker: Narrator
text: Names, dates, times. And in the margin, in a neat professor’s hand, a column of numbers that climbs by two each night: 4, 6, 8. Beside it, circled twice, the number 13.

speaker: Matron Hale
text: I’m afraid,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says at last, very quietly,

speaker: Matron Hale
text: that I’ve seen this before. Fifty years ago. I was a junior nurse in this wing. Nobody wrote it down. Nobody said a word.

speaker: Narrator
text: She straightens.

speaker: Matron Hale
text: Go and eat, Kringer. And find someone who remembers.

speaker: Matron Hale
text: Out,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Matron Hale, tight-lipped, and she steers you into the corridor with a hand between your shoulder blades. Her hand is shaking.

speaker: Narrator
text: Day two. The Great Hall is half empty. Eight chairs stand unused along the house tables, and nobody talks at full voice. The staff say the word illness often enough to make it sound rehearsed.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pip’s chair is one of the empty ones. Someone has left his spoon beside the plate, as if he might be back for it.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the staff table Professor Corvin Ashgrove, who teaches Defence Against the Dark Arts, sits with a cup of tea and a face you would like to trust. He catches your eye and nods, mild and kind.

speaker: Narrator
text: You pretend to read and watch the staff table over the edge of the page. Ashgrove’s tea has not been touched. His eyes keep drifting to the ceiling. Matron Hale isn’t eating either. And one chair stands empty: the caretaker’s. Harrow, who never misses a meal, is somewhere else.

speaker: Narrator
text: Professor Ashgrove listens with his whole face, nodding in all the right places, and when you finish he lays a hand on your shoulder.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: You were right to come to me, Kringer. This is something for adults to handle.

speaker: Narrator
text: His gaze drifts upward for a heartbeat, to the ceiling, to the tower beyond it, and returns.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: I need your word that you won’t go after that bell on your own, and that you won’t draw other students into this. For their safety. And yours.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela sits alone on the courtyard wall with a notebook full of times and the look of a person who has not slept since Monday. She raises an eyebrow as you tell her, then writes something down.

speaker: Mirela
text: The tower was sealed fifty years ago and there’s not a line in the school records about why,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says.

speaker: Mirela
text: I think I know how to stop it. I need someone with nerve.

speaker: Narrator
text: She considers you.

speaker: Mirela
text: Congratulations. You volunteered.

speaker: Narrator
text: On your way out of the Great Hall Harrow steps into your path. He has dark rings under his eyes and the look of a man who has not slept in days.

speaker: Harrow
text: You’re in my book, Kringer,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says dryly.

speaker: Harrow
text: One warning.

speaker: Narrator
text: He nods to you, almost as to an equal.

speaker: Narrator
text: His coat smells of pipe smoke and lamp oil, and when he clears his throat it is a hard, dry cough you have heard before.

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow goes very still.

speaker: Harrow
text: You followed someone with keys,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Harrow
text: And you think it was me.

speaker: Narrator
text: The old man does not shout, and that is worse.

speaker: Harrow
text: It was me,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says finally.

speaker: Harrow
text: Every night since the first sleeper. Because if somebody doesn’t watch that door, somebody worse than me will.

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow looks at you for a long time. Then he draws out his book, tears the page free, and folds it into his pocket.

speaker: Harrow
text: We’ll say no more about it,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Harrow
text: You’ve got enough on your plate.

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow glances up and down the corridor and lowers his voice.

speaker: Harrow
text: I was a junior caretaker the night it started, fifty years back. I saw a boy in an archive coat carry music out of the east wing and lock the door behind him. He was crying. I never asked who it was.

speaker: Harrow
text: I’ve watched that tower ever since. If you need something, Kringer, you come to me.

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow unhooks a heavy ring from his belt and twists a brass key free.

speaker: Harrow
text: Opens most doors in the east and west wings. You never had it, understand?

speaker: Narrator
text: He presses it into your palm and walks away without waiting for an answer.

speaker: Narrator
text: It is early afternoon. The bell will toll again tonight; everyone knows it, and everyone is pretending not to. You have until dusk, and time for two leads, not three.

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow’s warning sits in your pocket like a small cold stone.

speaker: Narrator
text: Across the courtyard Mirela catches your eye and taps her wrist, once: time.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela is waiting behind the greenhouses with a map of the castle and a long column of numbers: the times the bell has rung.

speaker: Mirela
text: I’ve done the arithmetic,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says.

speaker: Mirela
text: It’s speeding up. At this rate the whole castle is asleep in four days.

speaker: Mirela
text: I have a plan, and you won’t like it. I found a counter-spell in an old book that can break metal like this. We take the bell.

speaker: Narrator
text: She looks at you.

speaker: Mirela
text: But I don’t know what lies under that tower. I only know I can’t watch one more person fall asleep.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela bites her lip. Then, reluctantly, she nods.

speaker: Mirela
text: Fine. But if there’s nothing else by tonight, we take the bell. No more talking.

speaker: Narrator
text: She folds the map into her pocket, and you realise she was relieved. She never wanted to be the one deciding.

speaker: Mirela
text: Careful,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Mirela bitterly.

speaker: Mirela
text: We’ve had five careful days.

speaker: Narrator
text: She folds up the map, and her eyes are hard.

speaker: Mirela
text: I’ll do it with you or without you, Kringer.

speaker: Narrator
text: She walks away and leaves you standing between the greenhouses.

speaker: Narrator
text: The archive lies three flights beneath the kitchens: shelves to the ceiling, dust that glows in lantern light, a smell of old paper and cold stone. Behind an oak desk sits Quill, spectacles pushed up into his hair, apparently in the middle of an argument with a cat.

speaker: Narrator
text: He looks up and beams.

speaker: Quill
text: Ah! My night visitor. Sit. Mind the cat; she bites scholars.

speaker: Quill
text: You’re late,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Quill
text: Or early. It rather depends what you’re looking for.

speaker: Narrator
text: Quill sets down his pen and draws out a folder sealed with brown wax.

speaker: Quill
text: Hollow Bell. Cast three hundred years ago by Cantor Eadric Vale, who led the castle choir. It was never meant to warn anyone. It was meant to hold something down.

speaker: Quill
text: Beneath the tower lies what we call the Hush. It eats sound, and it eats sleep. Vale sang it to rest every night with a song that closes the bell. Then the song was lost, and the bell began to ring by itself. Now it feeds on whoever sleeps.

speaker: Narrator
text: He peers at you over the folder.

speaker: Quill
text: The song was written on two pages. I know where one of them is.

speaker: Narrator
text: While you leaf innocently through a crate of nineteenth-century accounts, you find a letter from Cantor Vale to the headmaster: The bell will ring itself if the song is forgotten. Remember that the song is written on two pages.

speaker: Narrator
text: Quill has been standing behind you the entire time.

speaker: Quill
text: You’re looking for the bell, aren’t you?

speaker: Narrator
text: He smiles thinly.

speaker: Quill
text: You look so innocent that you very nearly fooled me.

speaker: Narrator
text: Quill takes off his spectacles and rubs his eyes.

speaker: Quill
text: I wasn’t always an archivist. Fifty years ago I was Vale’s last student, seventeen years old. The night the bell began ringing by itself, I panicked. I tore out the page with the song and locked the music room. I thought that would stop it.

speaker: Quill
text: It did the opposite. Since then I have been an archivist, a watchman and a coward, all at once.

speaker: Narrator
text: He puts the spectacles back on, and his hands are not quite steady.

speaker: Narrator
text: Behind Quill the shelves hold a thousand folders, and some are dustier than others.

speaker: Quill
text: It’s in there somewhere,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Quill
text: I can’t search any more. My eyes aren’t what they were.

speaker: Narrator
text: Under a stack of old accounts you find a single page in neat, faded ink: the notes of a lullaby. Over them Vale has written: The Cantor’s close. To be sung from the tower, and the bell shall be stilled.

speaker: Narrator
text: The page is cold in your hand, but you feel it wants something. Quill nods.

speaker: Quill
text: Take it. And for heaven’s sake, don’t lose it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Quill closes his eyes. For a long moment nothing happens. Then, in a thin, cracked voice that has not sung in fifty years, he begins to hum. The melody is simple and very sad, and you find you already know where it is going.

speaker: Narrator
text: When he finishes he is crying and pretending not to.

speaker: Quill
text: That is as much as I have,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Quill
text: Mind it well.

speaker: Narrator
text: You search for hours. The paper crumbles between your fingers, and the ink has run where it is worst. In the end you find only an empty cover and the ragged edge of something torn out long ago.

speaker: Quill
text: Somebody got here first,

speaker: Narrator
text: Quill mutters.

speaker: Quill
text: It’s not the first time something has disappeared from here.

speaker: Narrator
text: The music room in the east wing has been locked for longer than anyone can say. The door is covered in frost flowers, though the day is mild. From behind it comes a hum: a very old melody, almost too faint to be real.

speaker: Narrator
text: The door swings open on its own. In the middle of the room, among overturned stools and a closed grand piano, stands a transparent man in a choir cassock, hands folded before him as if in prayer.

speaker: Vale
text: No one has knocked here in a very long time,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says, and his voice carries a strange harmonic, as though two people are speaking.

speaker: Vale
text: You are kind. Come in. I am Eadric Vale.

speaker: Narrator
text: The door splinters on its hinges, and cold pours out of the room. In the middle of it a transparent figure shoots up toward the ceiling, shrieking without sound.

speaker: Vale
text: You come to take more!

speaker: Narrator
text: he cries.

speaker: Vale
text: I have nothing left to give!

speaker: Narrator
text: You are Eadric Vale, three hundred years ago. It is night and the castle sleeps. Beneath the belfry floor you feel the Hush stirring like a hungry dog.

speaker: Narrator
text: You have cast a bell of black metal and written a song on two pages. You know it will work. You do not yet know what it will cost.

speaker: Narrator
text: The bell answers. The Hush sinks. But with every night you sing, you notice the power must come from somewhere: the students you teach sleep more heavily, and some of them never quite wake.

speaker: Wall voice
text: Every pact has a price,

speaker: Narrator
text: says a calm voice from the wall. It is not hostile. It is only honest.

speaker: Narrator
text: You blink, and the music room is back. Vale stands before you, and in his eyes you can see that he knows what you have seen.

speaker: Vale
text: Now you know why I cannot sing alone,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says quietly.

speaker: Vale
text: The song is true only if someone shares the price with me. I remember it all, child. The melody still lives in me. I merely cannot hold it up by myself.

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale speaks softly. He saved the castle once by making a pact: he would sing the Hush to rest every night, and the bell would hold it down. When he died the song stayed in him and bound him to this room. Then someone broke in and took half of the notes. Ever since, he has not been able to sing alone.

speaker: Narrator
text: He offers you a small silver fork that glows faintly.

speaker: Vale
text: My tuning fork. With it you can tune the bell to the lullaby. And if you find the pages, perhaps we can give them peace together.

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale turns away. As you press him, he tells it shortly and bitterly: the pact, the bell, the Hush, and the half of the notes that was stolen.

speaker: Vale
text: Now go,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says, and the door closes behind you.

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale looks toward the door.

speaker: Vale
text: There has been another here,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Vale
text: The professor. Three times. He wants the song, but not to close the bell. He wants to use it to ring thirteen.

speaker: Vale
text: I said no. But he promises me my freedom if I sing. I am tired, child. I am so very tired.

speaker: Narrator
text: Professor Ashgrove’s office is in the west wing behind a door of dark wood with a small brass nameplate. It is lunchtime, and the room beyond is dark: nobody is home.

speaker: Narrator
text: Through the keyhole you see a tidy desk, a glass cabinet of silver instruments, and an open book.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ashgrove comes up the corridor with his cloak over his arm and greets you with a warm smile. He lets you in, puts the kettle on, and listens. He is courteous, nearly too courteous.

speaker: Narrator
text: As he pours, you notice that the book on his desk lies open to a number circled in pencil: 13.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ashgrove looks down into his cup for a long time.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: My sister Lenora climbed Hollow Tower when she was twelve, to prove she was brave. She fell asleep up there. She never woke.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: I was sixteen. I have spent the rest of my life trying to understand why.

speaker: Narrator
text: His smile tightens.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: An old arithmetic exercise,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says, but his finger drums against the desk. After a long moment he adds, more quietly:

speaker: Ashgrove
text: Some doors should stay closed, Kringer. Trust me. I am trying to protect you.

speaker: Narrator
text: You see how afraid he is beneath the calm. It is not a villain’s fear. It is the fear of a man who has decided on something terrible.

speaker: Narrator
text: He walks you to the door, still smiling.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: Come to me whenever you’re worried.

speaker: Narrator
text: The door closes behind you, and you feel he was relieved that you did not ask.

speaker: Narrator
text: You slip inside and open the book. It is not a book. It is a ledger: rows of names, and beside each the date a student fell asleep. At the bottom, in the professor’s tidy hand: The Last Toll. Thirteen strokes. When the Hush is full, it seals for ever. The price: the sleepers’ sleep. They will not wake.

speaker: Narrator
text: A desk drawer is slightly ajar.

speaker: Narrator
text: You tuck the ledger under your cloak and are gone before anyone comes.

speaker: Narrator
text: Under a stack of letters lies a single sheet of music, brittle at the creases, written in Vale’s own hand. The other half of the song. He has had it all along.

speaker: Narrator
text: You take it, and the ledger, and leave the door exactly as you found it.

speaker: Narrator
text: You have barely opened the book when the door swings wide. Ashgrove stands in the opening, and his gaze is suddenly not warm any more.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: Interesting,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says quietly.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: Out.

speaker: Narrator
text: He writes something on a slip of paper. You are reported to the headmaster.

speaker: Narrator
text: Outside the staff room you hear Mirela’s voice, hard and controlled.

speaker: Mirela
text: You know more than you say, Professor. Fifteen students have fallen asleep since Monday.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ashgrove answers calmly, but his hands are white.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: You do not understand what you are saying, Miss Voss.

speaker: Narrator
text: You are the only one who sees them.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the archive door you hear Quill tell Mirela what he told you: that he tore out the page fifty years ago. Mirela goes quiet. Then she goes white.

speaker: Mirela
text: You knew why,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says.

speaker: Mirela
text: All this time?

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow and Quill stand in the corridor, snarling at each other in low voices.

speaker: Harrow
text: You locked the door and let us think it was an accident,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Harrow.

speaker: Quill
text: I was seventeen!

speaker: Narrator
text: Quill retorts. Both look up as you appear.

speaker: Narrator
text: Passing the music room you see the door standing ajar. Ashgrove is inside, his back to you.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: One more time,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says softly.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: Sing it, and I will set you free.

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale does not answer. He looks at you through the gap.

speaker: Narrator
text: Quill hands you a sealed envelope.

speaker: Quill
text: Give this to Corvin. He will understand.

speaker: Narrator
text: It is heavier than paper should be.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela has spoken to Harrow and is full of questions.

speaker: Mirela
text: You must have a way into the tower,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says.

speaker: Mirela
text: I want to check the tower door before tonight.

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow holds you back in a doorway.

speaker: Harrow
text: Tell Professor Ashgrove I can see he isn’t sleeping,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says quietly.

speaker: Harrow
text: And that I would rather have an honest man in that tower than a clever one.

speaker: Narrator
text: Somewhere below you someone coughs, a dry hard cough, and you realise you have been wondering all day who owns it. Harrow is two floors down, polishing a doorknob that does not need polishing.

speaker: Narrator
text: The sun sets behind Hollow Tower, and the tower throws a long shadow across the courtyard. In an hour the bell will toll. You go up to the dormitory to fetch what you need.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pip lies as he did last night: calm, cold, far away. On the bedside table sit a half-eaten chocolate frog and an unopened letter from his mother.

speaker: Narrator
text: Tonight the bell tolls earlier than yesterday, almost during supper. In two days more than thirty students have fallen asleep in their beds. The castle is closing its eyes.

speaker: Narrator
text: You go over what you know and what is in your pockets. What you did today decides what you must manage now.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela waits at the stairs with her wand in hand. She has not slept, and her gaze is sharp.

speaker: Mirela
text: What do we do if Ashgrove is up there?

speaker: Narrator
text: she asks quietly.

speaker: Mirela
text: If he’s the one ringing, he’s the enemy.

speaker: Narrator
text: You are Mirela. At the foot of the tower the silence has taken a shape: a tall, soundless shadow across the door. It turns toward you, though it has no head.

speaker: Narrator
text: Kringer has to get up the stairs. Your job is to hold it back. The notebook shakes in your hand.

speaker: Narrator
text: The shadow writhes, chokes, and draws back into the walls. You breathe out, shaking, and feel that something has changed: it does not fear you, but it respects you.

speaker: Narrator
text: You run up the stairs after Kringer.

speaker: Narrator
text: The spell dies in your mouth. The shadow swallows the sound, and your thoughts with it. You watch Kringer vanish up the stairs and want to shout, but you have no voice.

speaker: Narrator
text: The last thing you feel is the floor against your cheek. Then it goes very, very quiet.

speaker: Narrator
text: You slam the door and put your back against it. The shadow pounds, but it does not get through. You are safe, but you are going nowhere tonight.

speaker: Narrator
text: Kringer is alone up there.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Hollow Tower stair twists upward in the dark. The higher you climb, the thicker the silence grows: first your footsteps go, then your breath, then your thoughts. It is like wading through black wool.

speaker: Narrator
text: You hold on to the memory of sitting beside Pip, the warmth of his hand. It is something to keep hold of.

speaker: Narrator
text: A hundred steps remain. Somewhere above, the bell is waiting.

speaker: Narrator
text: The silence seizes you. You can no longer hear yourself. Your knees give way and the steps blur together. You are about to become part of it.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the top the stair opens into a round belfry with windows that have no glass, letting in night wind and mist. In the middle hangs the Hollow Bell: black, bigger than a cart, and humming so faintly that you feel it in your teeth.

speaker: Narrator
text: Professor Ashgrove stands by the ropes. He does not look surprised. In the corner, bound to the bell’s shadow by chains you cannot see, hangs Eadric Vale, almost lost in the light.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: You gave me your word,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Ashgrove, not unkindly.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: I did not ask you to come,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: But now that you are here, I can at least explain.

speaker: Vale
text: I promised,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Vale, and for the first time in three hundred years his chains snap. He flings himself between Ashgrove and the bell, and a cold wave throws the professor to the floor.

speaker: Vale
text: I am sorry,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Vale.

speaker: Vale
text: But this is what I owe them.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: The Hush beneath us is the only reason this castle still stands,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Ashgrove.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: Every night it grows stronger. The bell holds it down, but it feeds on the sleepers. If I ring thirteen strokes, it seals for ever. The price is those who already sleep.

speaker: Narrator
text: His voice cracks.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: Forty-one students for a thousand. I have done the arithmetic for ten years. I am not proud of it.

speaker: Narrator
text: He does not look at you as an enemy. He looks at you as someone who could stop him, and whom he hopes will not.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ashgrove is faster than you thought. His wand sends light and shadow flaring against the walls, and the silence takes the words out of your mouth. You wrestle for the rope while the bell hums in time with your heart.

speaker: Narrator
text: You seize the clapper in both hands and haul it down. Ashgrove falls to his knees, spent. The bell whines one last time and goes still.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: Don’t,

speaker: Narrator
text: he whispers.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: You don’t know what’s waiting below.

speaker: Narrator
text: But from the corner you hear Vale humming, thin and trembling. He needs you.

speaker: Narrator
text: The footsteps behind you are Quill’s. He has followed, pale and out of breath, lantern in hand.

speaker: Quill
text: Corvin,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says quietly.

speaker: Quill
text: It was I who tore out the page. It was I who locked the door. This is my responsibility. Don’t make it your students’.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela lays a hand on Quill’s shoulder. She says nothing, but she stands there.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela has drawn her wand.

speaker: Mirela
text: You let them sleep for fifty years,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says to Quill, and her voice shakes.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ashgrove stares at him. It is the first time you have seen him stop being calm.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: You?

speaker: Narrator
text: he whispers.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: All these years?

speaker: Narrator
text: Ashgrove lowers his hand. He sits in silence for a long moment.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: I have been set on this for ten years,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says at last.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: And a child comes and shows me I stopped looking for anything else.

speaker: Narrator
text: He steps aside, and for the first time Vale looks at you with hope.

speaker: Narrator
text: From inside his coat Ashgrove takes a folded sheet, brittle at the creases.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: I should have given you this long ago,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Ashgrove
text: The other half.

speaker: Narrator
text: Eadric Vale drifts out of the bell’s shadow.

speaker: Vale
text: If you ask me to sing, I bind myself to the bell once more. I do it gladly. But I need something to sing from.

speaker: Narrator
text: He no longer hides what he remembers. The melody is plainly in him, only waiting for something to hold it up.

speaker: Narrator
text: You walk toward the bell’s shadow. Vale looks up, afraid.

speaker: Vale
text: What are you doing?

speaker: Narrator
text: You know the words from the archive and from his story, and you say them aloud: the old pact, with your name on the Cantor’s line.

speaker: Narrator
text: The bell answers not with a toll but with something worse and kinder: attention. It knows who you are. The pact is waiting only for a yes.

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale takes the note from the fork, and his voice, old and clear, fills the belfry. As he sings you read the pages aloud, and the bell begins to answer: not with a hollow toll but with a calm, clear tone that you feel down to your toes.

speaker: Narrator
text: Beneath you the Hush turns in its sleep and sinks deeper. And for the first time in two days a real light comes through the windows: dawn.

speaker: Narrator
text: Only the last stroke remains. Someone must take the rope and ring it in time with the song.

speaker: Narrator
text: You and Ashgrove take hold of the rope at the same moment. The bell strikes one clean note, and the mist in the tower lifts like a heavy cloak. One by one the students open their eyes in their beds.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the dormitory Pip sits up and asks, confused, if it’s breakfast yet. Then he looks at you and says,

speaker: Pip
text: I heard you. You said my name.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the dormitory Pip sits up and asks, confused, if it’s breakfast yet.

speaker: Narrator
text: He adds that he dreamed someone was sitting beside him, and that it was warm.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela wakes too. It takes her three days to be herself again, and she refuses to say what she dreamed.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela stands at the tower door with tears in her eyes and a notebook torn in half. She smiles anyway.

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale remains in the music room, but he sings now every evening, softly, and the Hush sleeps. Quill puts the pages on display in the archive, behind glass.

speaker: Narrator
text: Before sunrise Ashgrove goes to the music room and asks Vale’s forgiveness. Vale answers with a note, and the two of them sing together for the first time in three hundred years.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ashgrove goes to the headmaster that same morning and tells him everything. He keeps his post, but he must apologise to every student, one by one.

speaker: Narrator
text: You sleep well tonight, Kringer.

speaker: Narrator
text: You take the rope alone and ring the last stroke in time with Vale’s voice. The bell answers with a note so pure that the glass in the tower sings. The Hush sinks, and the day comes.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ashgrove sits on the floor, broken. He looks at the bell and understands, too late, what he almost did. He leaves without a word, and nobody sees him again until autumn.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the dormitory Pip sits up.

speaker: Pip
text: I heard you,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Pip
text: I just couldn’t answer.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the dormitory Pip sits up and asks if it’s breakfast yet.

speaker: Narrator
text: He says he dreamed someone sat beside him, and that it was warm.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela wakes too, after three days. She no longer trusts anyone who smiles too much.

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow sits beside Ashgrove all night, saying nothing. It is enough.

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale stays in the music room and sings the Hush to rest each evening. The castle wakes, but you will always remember how close it was.

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale sings from memory. His voice is weaker than you expected, but it is true. The bell answers, and with every note he grows a little more transparent.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the last note he smiles.

speaker: Vale
text: Three hundred years,

speaker: Narrator
text: he says.

speaker: Vale
text: At last I am finished.

speaker: Narrator
text: He fades into the light that comes through the windows.

speaker: Narrator
text: The students wake, one by one. Pip asks if it’s breakfast yet. The castle is safe, but the song is gone for ever.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela wakes too, but it takes three days.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ashgrove sits in the tower long afterwards. He says nothing, but you see that he is weeping.

speaker: Vale
text: I should have stopped sooner,

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale says in the last moment.

speaker: Vale
text: Thank you for letting me do it right this time.

speaker: Vale
text: I sang to protect them,

speaker: Narrator
text: Vale whispers.

speaker: Vale
text: It is all I ever wanted.

speaker: Narrator
text: You and Mirela raise your wands together. The bell shatters with a sound that makes the whole castle shake. The Hush is loose. The walls tremble, the lights die, and far below something opens its eyes.

speaker: Narrator
text: The students wake that night, every one, in a castle evacuated before dawn. Hogwarts is closed for months.

speaker: Narrator
text: What lives beneath Hollow Tower now, nobody knows. It does not sing. It only listens.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pip is awake and well. He has not forgotten that you tried to wake him.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela looks away.

speaker: Mirela
text: You wanted us to wait,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says quietly. She says no more, but you know she hasn’t forgiven herself.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela smiles for the first time in days.

speaker: Mirela
text: I told you,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says. Then she looks down into the hole in the floor, and the smile fades.

speaker: Narrator
text: Harrow and Mirela stand together at the gate, receiving the evacuated students. It is the first time you have seen the caretaker laugh.

speaker: Narrator
text: You take the rope beside Ashgrove. Thirteen strokes. Each is heavier than the last, and after the final one you hear it: nothing. Not wind, not song, not breath.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Hush is sealed. The castle is safe. But the dormitories are full of students who will never wake.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pip lies in the bed beside yours. You know he heard you. It doesn’t help.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pip lies in the bed beside yours, dreaming on.

speaker: Narrator
text: You sat with him that evening. It is all you got.

speaker: Narrator
text: Mirela sleeps among them.

speaker: Narrator
text: You drift through the rest of your school years as if in a dream. Every night you hear the bell, though it never rings.

speaker: Narrator
text: There is no pain. The sound goes first, then the light, and finally your thoughts. You dream that you are standing in the belfry, ringing a bell that nobody can hear.

speaker: Narrator
text: The next morning there is one more student who does not wake.

speaker: Narrator
text: But inside the dream you remember everything. Perhaps you can find a way out.

speaker: Narrator
text: The headmaster reads the slip in silence.

speaker: Headmaster
text: Two warnings in two days, Kringer. I am sorry.

speaker: Narrator
text: You pack your trunk that evening. From the carriage you see Hollow Tower against the sky, the light at its top pulsing in time with your heart.

speaker: Narrator
text: At home you hear the bell in your dreams. You never learn whether anyone was ever saved.

speaker: Narrator
text: You say yes. The bell sings through you, and the pact moves from Vale to you. The Cantor smiles, almost embarrassed, and dissolves into light.

speaker: Narrator
text: The students wake, every one. Nobody knows why.

speaker: Narrator
text: From that night you are the castle’s bell-keeper. Every midnight you stand in the tower and sing the Hush to rest. You are never tired, never alone, and never quite awake.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pip notices that you never sleep. He says nothing, but he leaves a cup of tea on the stairs every evening.

speaker: Narrator
text: Snow has been falling on the castle since lunch, and the Great Hall has given up pretending to be a dining room. Tonight it is a ballroom: four hundred floating candles, a ceiling full of slow snow that never lands, and a string quartet of enchanted instruments that plays a little faster whenever a teacher walks past.

speaker: Narrator
text: It is Ingerid who notices it first. Behind the tapestry of the dancing trolls, where there has always been stone, there is a corridor. Its floor is polished like ice. At the far end, something catches the candlelight and throws it back.

speaker: Narrator
text: Madam Ottoline Pell, the librarian, is chaperoning tonight from a chair by the door with a book in her lap. She has not looked up in an hour.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ingerid takes Kristian's hand without a word and pulls. The tapestry trolls stop dancing to watch them go.

speaker: Ingerid
text: Wait here,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Ingerid, and takes three careful steps onto the icy floor, testing it like a frozen pond.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ingerid crosses the hall to Madam Pell, who listens, closes her book on one finger, and looks at the tapestry for a long moment.

speaker: Madam Pell
text: That corridor,

speaker: Narrator
text: she says quietly,

speaker: Madam Pell
text: was bricked up in 1923. Do not go far. I will be right behind you.

speaker: Narrator
text: The music behind them goes thin, as if it is being played in another room. The corridor smells of cold glass and old roses.

speaker: Narrator
text: The corridor opens into a long gallery of mirrors, floor to ceiling, each one taller than a door. Moonlight comes in from nowhere. In every mirror there are two of them, and then four, and then a hundred, all the way down into silver.

speaker: Narrator
text: Kristian's joke about haunted corridors echoes back from the glass a moment too late, in a voice that is almost his.

speaker: Narrator
text: Between two mirrors hangs a portrait of an old wizard asleep in an armchair, snoring gently. The brass plate reads: Sir Aldous Vane, Keeper of the Hall.

speaker: Narrator
text: Then one of the reflections of Kristian does not move when he moves. It tilts its head. It smiles, politely, the way a stranger smiles across a train carriage.

speaker: Gloam
text: Good evening,

speaker: Narrator
text: it says to Ingerid.

speaker: Gloam
text: You have no idea how long it has been since anyone came to the ball.

speaker: Ingerid
text: Who are you?

speaker: Narrator
text: asks Ingerid. The reflection bows.

speaker: Gloam
text: Leander Gloam,

speaker: Narrator
text: it says.

speaker: Gloam
text: Fifth year. Ravenclaw, once. I came to a ball like this one and I never quite left.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ingerid raps on the frame of the portrait. Sir Aldous wakes with a snort, sees the smiling reflection and goes white under his paint.

speaker: Sir Aldous
text: Do not give it your name!

speaker: Narrator
text: he cries.

speaker: Sir Aldous
text: Whatever it offers, girl, it must never have your name!

speaker: Narrator
text: Ingerid grabs Kristian's sleeve and holds on. In the confusion her scarf ends up wound around his wrist.

speaker: Narrator
text: The reflection turns to Kristian.

speaker: Gloam
text: And you,

speaker: Narrator
text: it says warmly.

speaker: Gloam
text: You look like someone who would understand. Come closer. The glass is cold, but it is honest.

speaker: Narrator
text: Kristian's fingertips meet the glass, and the glass does not stop them. It gives, like the skin of cold water.

speaker: Narrator
text: Kristian steps back, hard. It makes no difference. The floor tilts like the deck of a ship, and he slides toward the mirror as if the whole hall has decided it.

speaker: Kristian
text: Good evening,

speaker: Narrator
text: says Kristian, because his grandmother raised him properly. The reflection looks genuinely touched. Then the mirror opens like a door, and Kristian is on the other side of it.

speaker: Narrator
text: There is no sound. There is no flash. One moment Kristian is standing next to Ingerid; the next he is standing next to her in the mirror, and nowhere else.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ingerid's scarf has gone with him. She can see the end of it trailing from his wrist, in the glass.

speaker: Narrator
text: He presses his hands to the glass from the inside. His mouth moves. Ingerid cannot hear a single word.

speaker: Narrator
text: On the other side of the glass the castle is exactly the same and completely wrong. The candles burn downward. The tapestry trolls dance backwards. Every word on every sign is written the wrong way round, and the snow outside the windows falls up.

speaker: Narrator
text: There is no colour here, only silver and grey and the deep blue of moonlight. Kristian's own footsteps reach his ears a heartbeat before he takes them.

speaker: Narrator
text: He still has Ingerid's scarf around his wrist. It is the only warm colour in the whole world.

speaker: Narrator
text: Through the mirror he can see Ingerid, small and real and very far away, in a hall full of ordinary candlelight.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the end of the silver gallery, a figure in old-fashioned school robes beckons to him, and then slips round a corner.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ingerid stands alone in the Hall of Glass. The quartet in the Great Hall has started a waltz. Nobody has noticed that two students are missing.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the mirror, Kristian is crouching, picking something up from the silver floor: a long, sharp sliver of glass that glows faintly. He holds it up so she can see.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the mirror, Kristian walks the length of the silver gallery and back again, twice, and each time ends up exactly where he started. He looks very tired of it.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the mirror, Kristian hurries after a figure in old school robes, and the two of them vanish round a corner. A minute later Kristian comes back alone, looking thoughtful.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the mirror, Kristian breathes on the glass and writes in the mist with one finger. The letters come out backwards on her side, but she can read them: ARE YOU OK? HOW DO I GET BACK?

speaker: Sir Aldous
text: The hall opens at midnight,

speaker: Narrator
text: mutters Sir Aldous from his frame,

speaker: Sir Aldous
text: on the last stroke, and only if both sides turn together. That is all I know, and it is a great deal more than I should.

speaker: Narrator
text: The great clock above the ballroom says a quarter past eleven. Every story Ingerid has ever heard about this castle's lost hall ends the same way: whoever is still inside at the last stroke of midnight stays inside for a hundred years.

speaker: Narrator
text: She has three quarters of an hour to get Kristian back.

speaker: Narrator
text: For a few minutes the mirror becomes a slate. Ingerid writes, Kristian writes back. It is slow, and every word has to be read backwards, and it is the best conversation either of them has had all year.

speaker: Narrator
text: They agree on one thing, in capitals, underlined twice: whatever happens, they will act together on the twelfth stroke of midnight. TWELVE, writes Kristian. TWELVE, writes Ingerid.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the real hall, Ingerid is gone, running. Kristian watches her go and feels, for the first time, properly alone.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the real hall, Ingerid stands perfectly still and watches him, not blinking, like a cat at a window. It helps more than he would have guessed.

speaker: Narrator
text: On the glass, in her handwriting, backwards from his side: HOLD ON. I'M HERE.

speaker: Narrator
text: The silver castle goes on and on. Kristian walks into a gallery of portraits, every one of them the reflection of a painting he has walked past a hundred times. Here, the painted people are awake, and they are all looking at him.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the far end, somewhere beyond the portraits, a music box is playing a waltz, very slowly, as if it is running down. Above him, a door stands open onto a balcony where the snow is falling the wrong way.

speaker: Narrator
